You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the test sets up:
  - It integrates the simple harmonic oscillator y' = [y1, -y0] whose solution is [sin(t), cos(t)].
  - It registers two event handlers/step handlers:
    - sinChecker for y[0] (sin) expected to fire at 0, π, 2π, …
    - cosChecker for y[1] (cos) expected to fire at π/2, 3π/2, …
  - The test checks that events are scheduled/handled correctly when both handlers are active.

- Relevant event-handling flow in the integrator:
  - During each accepted step, AbstractIntegrator.acceptStep:
    - Initializes EventState instances on first entry (reinitializeBegin).
    - Collects all events that would occur in the current step into a set occuringEvents (by calling EventState.evaluateStep on each handler).
    - Processes the earliest event:
      - Restricts the step to the event time.
      - Calls currentEvent.stepAccepted(eventT, eventY).
      - If the handler requests a stop, it updates remaining occuringEvents via stepAccepted and returns.
      - Otherwise, it calls currentEvent.reset(eventT, eventY). If this returns needReset = true, it:
        - Copies the event state into y, recomputes derivatives, marks resetOccurred,
        - Calls stepAccepted(eventT, eventY) only for the remaining handlers in occuringEvents,
        - Returns early to the main integration loop.

- Where the bug occurs:
  - In the “needReset” branch inside AbstractIntegrator.acceptStep, the code returns immediately after handling the current event and updating only the other handlers that had pending events in the same step (the occuringEvents set).
  - It does not advance the EventState of handlers that did not have an event in the current step. Those EventState instances are left with their internal state (t0, g0, sign) corresponding to the beginning of the step, not the event time.
  - As a consequence, when the next step starts (after the RESET_STATE was applied), some EventState objects still think the “previous time” and g-value are from before the reset event. Their internal brackets/signs are out of sync with the now-reset ODE state.

- Why this breaks the test:
  - With two independent event handlers (sin and cos), if one of them triggers an Action.RESET_STATE in its eventOccurred, the other handler must also be brought forward to the same event time so its g(t,y) and sign are consistent with the new integration state.
  - Due to the early return path, the other handler(s) are not updated unless they also had an event scheduled in that same step. This leads to incorrect scheduling in subsequent steps (e.g., missed or misordered crossings), which causes the test that checks coordinated event scheduling to fail.

- Code evidence supporting the diagnosis:
  - AbstractIntegrator.acceptStep:
    - Calls currentEvent.stepAccepted(eventT, eventY) once the event time is reached.
    - If needReset is true, it only calls stepAccepted for “remaining” events in occuringEvents, then returns. It does not call stepAccepted on all eventsStates.
  - EventState.stepAccepted updates the internal time/sign by evaluating g at the accepted time. Skipping this call for non-occuring events leaves them stale across a RESET_STATE.

In short: When one event handler triggers RESET_STATE, other event handlers that did not have a pending event in that step are not advanced to the event time due to an early return in the integrator. This leaves their EventState inconsistent with the reset integration state, causing incorrect event scheduling in the next step and making the test fail.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
